summary: Presents a performance evaluation of the Maximum Allocation and Russian Dolls bandwidth constraints models described in RFC 3564 for Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering. It examines how the two models behave under different operating conditions, such as blocking and preemption of label switched paths. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Networks that treat traffic in priority classes need rules for how much bandwidth each class may claim. This memo tests the two candidate rules and reports where each one works well and where it fails.

questions: how do mpls bandwidth constraints work
when to use russian dolls or maximum allocation model
what is a bandwidth constraint model
subtitle: Testing two bandwidth allocation schemes for prioritized network traffic, and reporting where each one works.

tldr.problem: Networks that serve several priority classes of traffic need rules for how much bandwidth each class may claim, so that high-priority traffic is not starved and capacity is not wasted.
tldr.mechanism: Two models are compared. The Russian Dolls Model stacks the classes inside one another so unused bandwidth flows down, while the Maximum Allocation Model gives each class its own limit. Both are tested under normal load, overload, partial preemption, blocking and complete sharing.
tldr.outcome: Russian Dolls shares bandwidth more efficiently but couples the classes together, while Maximum Allocation isolates classes better but wastes capacity. The memo advises choosing from the provider's own service requirements rather than reusing the other model's numbers.

today: RFC 4128 is an Informational memo published in June 2005, and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It is a companion to the requirements document RFC 3564, which defines the two bandwidth constraint models it evaluates.

sections.title: What the Document Sets Out to Test
sections.content:
Differentiated Services-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering (DS-TE) works on the basis of different traffic classes, so that the network can improve performance for each of them. To engineer per class rather than across all classes at once, DS-TE enforces different Bandwidth Constraints (BCs) on different classes. This document evaluates the two Bandwidth Constraints Models (BCMs) described in RFC 3564, under normal load, overload, preemption fully or partially enabled, pure blocking, and complete sharing.

The selection criteria listed in RFC 3564 cover the scenarios, behaviour under normal and overload conditions, preemption, signalling load, efficient use of the network, and implementation complexity. This document deliberately addresses only three of them: working well under both normal and overload conditions, applying equally whether preemption is enabled or disabled, and maximizing efficient use of the network. The choice of model has a significant effect on a network's ability to protect different classes of traffic under high load, which is what makes the evaluation worth doing.

The memo also notes a difference between Diffserv with and without DS-TE. Diffserv does not indicate preemption, by intent, while DS-TE describes several levels of preemption for its class types, and Diffserv offers no means of explicitly controlling overbooking, while DS-TE allows it.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks that serve traffic in priority classes need rules for how much bandwidth each class may claim. This memo tests the two candidate rules and reports where each one works well and where it fails.

sections.title: The Two Bandwidth Constraint Models
sections.content:
The Maximum Allocation Model (MAM) sets an explicit maximum on how much bandwidth each class may use, and separately on the aggregate use across all classes. The Russian Dolls Model (RDM) specifies the maximum cumulatively, by grouping successive priority classes recursively, so the classes sit inside one another like nesting dolls.

The analysis assumes three traffic classes, with class 1 the highest priority and class 3 the lowest, and that every label switched path uses the same amount of bandwidth. Each path is treated as one unit of bandwidth on a link, so link usage can be expressed as the number of simultaneously established paths. Let Nmax be the link capacity and Nc the number of established paths of class c.

Under MAM, Bc is the maximum number of established class c paths, with Nc at most Bc and at most Nmax for each class, N1 plus N2 plus N3 at most Nmax, and B1 plus B2 plus B3 at least Nmax. Under RDM, B1 is the maximum for class 1 alone, B2 the maximum for classes 1 and 2 together, and B3 the maximum for all three together, with B1 less than B2 less than B3 equal to Nmax. The ordering is the important difference: RDM has a hard boundary at the link capacity, while MAM has a soft one and no fixed order among the classes.
sections.plainLanguage: The two models differ in how they count. The Maximum Allocation Model gives each class its own allowance. The Russian Dolls Model counts each class together with the classes above it, so a lower-priority class only gets what the higher ones are not using.

sections.title: The Performance Model and the Example Link
sections.content:
The performance model comes from an earlier analysis of a general class of bandwidth constraint models, and it assumes Poisson arrivals of path requests with exponentially distributed lifetimes. The model uses admission control to allocate link bandwidth to paths of different classes according to their constraints. It takes the link capacity and the offered load per class as input and produces the blocking and preemption probabilities for each class as output, so a provider can run it repeatedly to find the set of constraints that gives a desired level of blocking and preemption.

Performance is measured by the probability that a path setup request is blocked or preempted. Preemption may be on or off, and only cross-class preemption is considered: class 1 can preempt class 3 or class 2, in that order, and class 2 can preempt class 3. The load of each class is expressed in erlangs, the arrival rate of path requests multiplied by the average lifetime of a path, which measures resource use independently of link speed.

The worked example is a link that can carry at most 15 paths at once, with each path lasting one time unit on average, offered 2.7 erlangs of class 1 traffic, 3.5 erlangs of class 2 and 3.5 erlangs of class 3. The constraints are chosen to give the three classes comparable blocking and preemption performance under normal conditions: for MAM, up to 6 paths for class 1, 7 for class 2 and 15 for class 3; for RDM, up to 6 for class 1 alone, 11 for classes 1 and 2 together, and 15 for all three. Under those conditions the two models behave almost the same: class 1 sees a blocking probability of 0.03692 in both, and the combined blocking and preemption figures for the three classes are very close. The small difference in favour of RDM comes from the cascaded arrangement, which gives class 3 some protection from being preempted. Compared with a single class, where 15 servers can carry an offered load of 10 erlangs with a blocking probability of 0.0364969, the three-class total load of 9.7 erlangs has higher blocking and preemption probabilities, so partitioning the link costs some efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: The test uses one link that holds 15 paths and three priority classes of traffic. Both models are given limits that produce the same quality for all three classes in normal conditions, and in those conditions they perform almost identically.

sections.title: Overload, Partial Preemption, Blocking and Complete Sharing
sections.content:
Under overload, with the load of one class raised above its normal level, both models degrade for the class whose load rises. Class 1 is unaffected by changes in the other classes because it can always preempt, and class 2 is unaffected by changes in class 3. The models differ in how class 2 reacts to class 1. Under MAM, class 2 sees almost no effect, because with limits of 6 and 7 the two classes are effectively served from separate pools and only class 3 is preempted. Under RDM the probability of class 2 being preempted by class 1 is not zero, because class 2 shares a limit with class 1 while class 3 is partly shielded by the cascade. The conclusion is that the sharing which makes RDM work better under normal conditions makes it less effective at isolating classes under overload.

When a provider wants class 2 to do better than class 3, it raises the class 2 limit: 9 for MAM and 13 for RDM in the example. Class 1 stays the same, class 2 improves and class 3 gets worse. The memo also asks whether this could lock class 3 out entirely. Under MAM with limits of 6, 9 and 15, a link holding 6 class 1 and 9 class 2 paths leaves no room for class 3. The same offered load does not lock class 3 out under RDM with a combined limit of 13, but class 2 requests are rejected instead. The memo's answer is that a provider engineers limits against projected demand, so treating an overload as the normal operating point is not realistic.

With preemption only partly enabled, RDM is sensitive to which classes may preempt which. If class 2 is not preemptable, class 1 sees higher blocking because it cannot reclaim space taken by class 2, and class 3 is preempted more often. MAM is relatively insensitive to the preemption mode, because each class has its own limits and the interference between classes is reduced.

With preemption disabled entirely, the cascaded arrangement works against the operator. Under RDM with the usual cascade, higher-priority traffic ends up with higher blocking than lower-priority traffic, the opposite of what is wanted, and reversing the cascade fixes that. Under MAM, giving class 1 a small private pool improves its blocking when its traffic is above normal, at a slight cost to classes 2 and 3.

With complete sharing, where every class may use the whole link, the two models become the same thing. Class 1 then sees almost no blocking, class 2 sees some, and class 3 suffers most, because higher-priority classes always preempt it when the link is full. Class 3 is starved under overload, with no protection at all.
sections.plainLanguage: The models part company when the network is overloaded. The model that shares bandwidth does better in normal conditions but lets one class suffer when another is busy. The model that keeps classes apart protects them but wastes capacity.

sections.title: Conclusions and the Sharing-Isolation Trade-Off
sections.content:
The overall theme is a trade-off between sharing bandwidth, which raises efficiency, and isolating classes, which protects them. Measured by the overall loss probability, the proportion of path requests from all classes lost to blocking or preemption, Complete Sharing is best on a single link and MAM is worst, with RDM in between. Complete Sharing also has the poorest class protection capability, and its overall loss probability is identical to that of a single class computed with the Erlang loss formula.

Sharing more bandwidth between classes raises link efficiency, but it also couples the classes more tightly. With the link properly dimensioned for each class, that coupling matters little under normal loading. Under overload, when capacity is scarce, the coupling is unavoidable and can severely degrade service for the lower-priority classes. The criterion that favors the most efficient use of the network therefore has to be applied with care; using it alone would lead straight to Complete Sharing.

The properties of the two models are summarized at the end. RDM allows greater sharing of bandwidth among the classes and performs somewhat better under normal conditions. It works well when preemption is fully enabled, but under partial preemption not all modes work equally well. MAM does not depend on the use of preemption, is relatively insensitive to the different preemption modes, and provides more robust class isolation under overload. In general, using preemption gives higher-priority traffic some immunity to the overloading of other classes, and the price is a higher blocking or preemption figure for the overloaded class than there would be in a pure blocking environment. The memo's advice is that the numbers designed for one model should not be adopted for the other; the service requirements, and perhaps the operational needs, of the provider should drive the choice.
sections.plainLanguage: The advice at the end is simple. Sharing bandwidth raises efficiency but couples the classes; keeping classes apart protects them but wastes capacity. Pick the model from your own service requirements, not from the numbers in the other model's examples.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document introduces no additional security threats beyond those already described for Diffserv and MPLS traffic engineering, and the same security measures and procedures apply here. The approach for defending against theft and denial of service attacks, which combines traffic conditioning at Diffserv boundary nodes with security and integrity of the network infrastructure inside a Diffserv domain, can be followed when DS-TE is in use.

One point is called out: manipulation of administratively configurable parameters, such as those related to DS-TE paths, has to be carried out in a secure manner by authorized entities. Preemption is such a parameter, and its values must be set correctly throughout the network. A misconfiguration in any label switch may cause new path setup requests to be blocked, or to preempt paths that are already established, and the preemption values in path setup requests must be configured properly as well, since otherwise they may affect the operation of existing paths.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo adds no new security threats. It does warn that the preemption settings are powerful: if they are wrong on one router, new paths can be blocked or can knock out paths that are already running.
